Yes, he really said it. But the clip is from 2024, not this election cycle, and it's missing some context.

**The quote is real.** Snopes checked it and rated it "Correct Attribution." 
Trump made the "everybody gets healthcare" comment while delivering remarks about affordability at his Bedminster, New Jersey, golf course on Aug. 15, 2024.
 His exact word was "everybody," not "everyone," but that doesn't change the meaning.

**The timing is misleading.** It went viral again in mid-October 2026. Some posts presented it as a new warning about the upcoming midterms. 
For example, one widely shared post said that Trump has warned that, if Democrats win the upcoming midterm elections, the US will be thrown into a "system where everybody gets healthcare".
 In fact, 
he made the remark months ahead of the 2024 election while urging voters not to vote for his opponent, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris.


**What he was talking about.** He was attacking single-payer health care, the idea of replacing private insurance with one government plan. Just before the line, he said Harris 
"cosponsored legislation to abolish very popular private health insurance, which 150 [million] Americans rely on, dumping everyone onto inferior socialist government run health care systems with rationing and deadly wait times, while massively raising your taxes."
 He then said people 
wanting to spend on "a really good plan, better than a government plan could be, far better, and you're not going to be allowed."
 Next came: 
"You're all going to be thrown into a communist system. It's a communist system. You're going to be thrown into a system where everybody gets healthcare. It's, you wait for your doctor like 10 months, 12 months, 11 months."


So he meant it as a warning about government-run health care and long waits. Even so, the phrase he used made it sound like universal coverage itself was the problem. Rolling Stone also pointed out that 
Harris did previously support eliminating private health insurance in favor of enacting "Medicare for All," or a universal health insurance program. She has since backed away from this idea.


**Bottom line:** Trump did say it, but in August 2024 about Kamala Harris, not about the 2026 midterms.

La frase tiene dos partes:

1. **“Vamos a mantener las pensiones públicas y actualizarlas con el IPC”**

2. **“Lo que hemos votado siempre / cada vez que nos lo han puesto encima de la mesa”**  
   → Esto sí se puede contrastar con votaciones. Y ahí aparecen excepciones claras: 2021, 2025 y enero de 2026.

Por eso concluí que la frase es **auténtica**, pero que la afirmación sobre haberlo votado “siempre” es **engañosa o inexacta**.

El PP apoya la indexación al IPC en principio (Pacto de Toledo) y dice apoyarla cuando se vota de forma aislada. ## In short: no, that's not true

Solar panels **slow down** global warming, because they replace electricity from fossil fuels. This myth does, however, have several sources that are worth discussing.

### Where does this myth come from?

**1. Emissions from production**
Producing panels requires energy, and in China, where most of them are made, a large share of it comes from coal. A panel, however, "pays back" this energy debt after about 1–3 years of operation, depending on insolation. It operates for 25–30 years or longer.
- The full life cycle of photovoltaics is about **20–50 g CO₂ per kWh**
- For coal it is about **800–1000 g CO₂ per kWh**, i.e. roughly 20–40 times more
- Natural gas is about **400–500 g CO₂ per kWh**

**2. The albedo effect (dark surface)**
Dark panels reflect less light than, for example, a bright desert or snow, so they absorb a little more heat. This is a real physical phenomenon, but scientific analyses show that on a global scale it is **negligible** compared with the benefit of reducing CO₂ emissions. That benefit outweighs it many times over. It is also worth remembering that panels convert part of the solar energy into electricity, which would otherwise end up in the surroundings as heat.

**3. Local "heat island effect"**
Studies show that large photovoltaic farms can slightly raise the temperature in their immediate surroundings, especially at night. This is a **local** effect, not a global one. There have also been model simulations of extreme scenarios, for example covering a large part of the Sahara with panels, pointing to regional climate changes. These, however, are theoretical considerations that do not apply to the current scale of installations.

### Conclusion
Every kilowatt-hour from photovoltaics that replaces electricity from coal or gas means less CO₂ in the atmosphere. The net balance is clearly favourable for the climate. Photovoltaics also has real problems, for example recycling used panels, extracting raw materials or the instability of output. Accelerating global warming is not one of them.

**No, that's not true.** Solar panels reduce global warming. This myth does, however, have several sources that are worth discussing.

## Where does this myth come from?

**1. Emissions from production**
Producing panels (purifying silicon, aluminium, glass, transport) does indeed cause CO₂ emissions, especially when factories use electricity from coal, as is often the case in China. But:
- Over the whole life cycle, photovoltaics emits an estimated **approx. 20–50 g CO₂ per kWh**.
- Coal is **approx. 800–1000 g/kWh**, and natural gas **approx. 400–500 g/kWh**.
- A panel "pays back" the energy used to produce it in **approx. 1–3 years**, and operates for **25–30 years and longer**.

**2. The albedo effect (dark surface)**
Panels are dark and absorb more light than e.g. bright sand or snow. This can locally raise the temperature (the so-called PV farm "heat island"). Analyses show, however, that this heating is **many times smaller** than the benefit of avoiding CO₂ emissions from burning fossil fuels. On building roofs the effect is practically negligible.

**3. Industrial gases**
Some stages of production use fluorinated gases (e.g. NF₃), which strongly warm the climate. Their share of the total carbon footprint is, however, small, and the industry is getting better and better at limiting their leaks.

**4. "Panels heat the air"**
Almost all the electricity consumed turns into heat anyway, regardless of its source. Coal and gas power plants release much more waste heat into their surroundings. On top of that, they emit CO₂, which traps heat for centuries. It is precisely CO₂, and not direct heat, that is responsible for global warming.

## What is the real problem?
Photovoltaics has real environmental challenges, but they do not consist in accelerating warming:
- recycling of used panels,
- extraction of raw materials,
- land use for large farms.

**Summary:** Every kilowatt-hour from panels that replaces electricity from coal or gas means a dozen or so to several dozen times fewer emissions. The balance for the climate is decidedly favourable.

**W skrócie: nie — to nieprawda w sensie globalnym.** Panele słoneczne mogą **lokalnie** zmieniać temperaturę powierzchni, bo są ciemne, pochłaniają światło i mogą obniżać albedo, szczególnie gdy zastępują jasny grunt, np. pustynny. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/?utm_source=openai))

Są trzy różne kwestie, które często się miesza:

([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Chapter06.pdf?utm_source=openai))

To jednak jest **mikroklimat / skala lokalna**, a nie dowód, że fotowoltaika przyspiesza globalne ocieplenie. ([journals.ametsoc.org](https://journals.ametsoc.org/abstract/journals/apme/58/5/jamc-d-18-0271.1.xml?utm_source=openai))

3. **Panele zmieniają albedo Ziemi** — tak, ale skala globalna jest mała. Gdy montuje się je na dachach, parkingach, terenach zdegradowanych albo w systemach z roślinnością pod panelami, efekt może być ograniczony, a czasem lokalnie korzystny przez zacienienie. Najgorszy wariant to wielkie instalacje na bardzo jasnych powierzchniach bez przemyślenia wpływu na grunt i ekosystem. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13544305/?utm_source=openai))

Poprawniej byłoby powiedzieć: **źle zaprojektowane farmy PV mogą lokalnie podnosić temperaturę, ale globalnie fotowoltaika pomaga ograniczać ocieplenie, jeśli zastępuje energię z paliw kopalnych.**

## Co wiedziałem przed wyszukiwaniem

Przed wyszukiwaniem wiedziałem ogólnie, że:

1. **Fotowoltaika ma emisje w cyklu życia**, bo produkcja paneli, aluminium, szkła, krzemu, transport i montaż zużywają energię. Nie jest więc „zeroemisyjna” w sensie całego cyklu życia.

4. **To nie oznacza automatycznie przyspieszania globalnego ocieplenia**, bo globalne ocieplenie jest przede wszystkim skutkiem trwałego wzrostu koncentracji gazów cieplarnianych. Jeśli PV zastępuje prąd z paliw kopalnych, zwykle zmniejsza emisje CO₂.

5. **Znałem też ogólny wniosek IPCC**, że efekt albedo związany z ciemnymi panelami jest mały w porównaniu z korzyścią klimatyczną wynikającą z redukcji emisji.

Czyli przed wyszukiwaniem znałem **ramę fizyczną i główny konsensus**: lokalne efekty cieplne — tak; globalne przyspieszanie ocieplenia — zasadniczo nie, jeśli PV wypiera paliwa kopalne.

## Co sprawdziłem po wyszukiwaniu

Po wyszukiwaniu sprawdziłem przede wszystkim trzy rzeczy: **emisje w cyklu życia**, **wpływ albedo/lokalnego ogrzewania** i **ocenę IPCC dotyczącą bilansu globalnego**.

### 1. IPCC AR6 WGIII — rozdział o systemach energetycznych

To było dla mnie najważniejsze źródło, bo IPCC syntetyzuje literaturę naukową. IPCC stwierdza, że fotowoltaika ma znacznie niższe emisje CO₂ na jednostkę energii niż energetyka kopalna, a obawy o systemowy efekt zmniejszenia albedo przez ciemne panele są „trywialne”/małe w porównaniu z korzyściami mitygacyjnymi. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/))

Z tego źródła pochodził główny wniosek: **panele mogą mieć lokalne skutki radiacyjne, ale globalnie ich efekt klimatyczny jest korzystny, gdy zastępują paliwa kopalne**.

### 2. NREL — porównanie emisji w cyklu życia

Użyłem też danych NREL / opracowania NREL o emisjach w cyklu życia technologii energetycznych. Podaje ono przykładowe wartości rzędu ok. **45 g CO₂e/kWh** dla krzemowej fotowoltaiki, wobec ok. **980 g CO₂e/kWh** dla węgla i ok. **450 g CO₂e/kWh** dla elektrowni gazowej typu combined-cycle. ([nrel.gov](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy15osti/63604.pdf))

To źródło potwierdzało liczbowo, dlaczego sama produkcja paneli nie zmienia wniosku: **PV ma emisje, ale dużo mniejsze niż elektrownie kopalne**.

### 3. IEA PVPS — ocena środowiskowego cyklu życia PV

Sprawdziłem też materiał IEA PVPS dotyczący środowiskowej oceny cyklu życia fotowoltaiki. Wskazuje on, że główne emisje PV pochodzą z produkcji, ale emisje są znacznie niższe niż w przypadku generatorów opartych na paliwach kopalnych, a nowsze technologie poprawiły wyniki w porównaniu ze starszymi danymi. ([iea-pvps.org](https://iea-pvps.org/fact-sheets/fact-sheet-environmental-life-cycle-assessment-of-electricity-from-pv-systems/))

To było źródło pomocnicze do stwierdzenia: **panele nie są bezkosztowe środowiskowo, ale ich ślad węglowy jest niski względem paliw kopalnych**.

### 4. Badania o lokalnym ogrzewaniu i „photovoltaic heat island”

Sprawdziłem badania o lokalnych efektach cieplnych. Jedno z badań terenowych wskazuje, że instalacje PV mogą powodować cieplejsze warunki przy powierzchni, szczególnie gdy są umieszczane nad jasnym, pustynnym gruntem o wyższym albedo. ([journals.ametsoc.org](https://journals.ametsoc.org/abstract/journals/apme/58/5/jamc-d-18-0271.1.xml))

Inne prace pokazują, że efekt zależy od miejsca: na jasnym gruncie panele mogą zwiększać pochłanianie energii, ale na dachach, parkingach lub powierzchniach miejskich sytuacja może być bardziej złożona, bo dochodzi zacienienie, zmiana strumieni ciepła i ograniczenie nagrzewania samego dachu. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13544305/))

To potwierdziło bardziej ostrożną wersję odpowiedzi: **lokalne ogrzewanie jest możliwe i realne, ale nie jest tym samym co globalne przyspieszanie ocieplenia**.

### 5. Źródła o albedo i bilansie energetycznym Ziemi

Dla ogólnej fizyki klimatu istotne jest, że zmiany albedo wpływają na ilość pochłanianego promieniowania słonecznego, a efekt cieplarniany wpływa na wypromieniowywanie energii w podczerwieni. IPCC WG1 opisuje bilans energetyczny Ziemi i znaczenie albedo w systemie klimatycznym. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/))

To źródło wspierało część fizyczną: **ciemna powierzchnia może pochłaniać więcej energii, ale skala, miejsce i porównanie z unikniętymi emisjami decydują o globalnym bilansie**.

## Najkrótsze podsumowanie źródeł

| Źródło | Do czego go użyłem |
|---|---|
| **IPCC AR6 WGIII, rozdział 6** | Główny wniosek: PV ma dużo niższe emisje niż paliwa kopalne; efekt albedo jest mały wobec korzyści klimatycznych. |

**In short: no — it is not true in the global sense.** Solar panels can **locally** change surface temperature, because they are dark, absorb light and can lower albedo, especially when they replace bright ground, e.g. desert. But in the climate balance they **usually reduce global warming**, because they produce electricity with much lower greenhouse gas emissions than coal and gas. The IPCC explicitly assesses that concerns about a global effect of reduced albedo from dark panels are **small compared with the climate benefits** of replacing fossil fuels. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/?utm_source=openai))

There are three different issues that are often mixed up:

1. **Producing panels emits CO₂** — yes, because raw materials have to be mined and silicon, glass, aluminium etc. have to be manufactured. But "cradle-to-grave" emissions are much lower than for fossil power plants. The IPCC gives typically tens of g CO₂/kWh for photovoltaics, while coal and gas have hundreds to approx. a thousand g CO₂/kWh; NREL gives, for example, approx. **45 g CO₂e/kWh** for silicon PV, versus approx. **980 g** for coal and **450 g** for CCGT gas. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Chapter06.pdf?utm_source=openai))

2. **Panels can locally heat the air or surface** — sometimes, yes. Field and modelling studies show a so-called local "photovoltaic heat island" effect, especially on dry, bright terrain, where panels absorb more radiation than the ground they replaced. This, however, is **microclimate / local scale**, and not proof that photovoltaics accelerates global warming. ([journals.ametsoc.org](https://journals.ametsoc.org/abstract/journals/apme/58/5/jamc-d-18-0271.1.xml?utm_source=openai))

3. **Panels change the Earth's albedo** — yes, but the global scale is small. When they are mounted on roofs, car parks, degraded land or in systems with vegetation under the panels, the effect may be limited, and sometimes locally beneficial through shading. The worst variant is huge installations on very bright surfaces without thinking through the impact on the ground and ecosystem. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13544305/?utm_source=openai))

**Conclusion:** solar panels **are not zero-emission and are not completely neutral locally**, but the claim that they "accelerate global warming" is fundamentally false. It would be more accurate to say: **poorly designed PV farms can locally raise temperature, but globally photovoltaics helps limit warming if it replaces energy from fossil fuels.**

You are right that it is worth asking "from where?". My answer was based on **general knowledge I already had beforehand** and on **checking scientific/institutional sources in a search**.

## What I knew before searching

Before searching, I knew in general that:

1. **Photovoltaics has life-cycle emissions**, because the production of panels, aluminium, glass and silicon, transport and installation consume energy. So it is not "zero-emission" in the sense of the whole life cycle.

2. **Despite this, PV emissions per 1 kWh are much lower than from coal and gas**, especially when a panel operates for several decades.

3. **Panels can change the local heat balance**, because they are dark, have low albedo and absorb a lot of solar radiation. This can lead to a local heating effect, especially on bright, dry surfaces.

4. **This does not automatically mean accelerating global warming**, because global warming is primarily the result of a lasting increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases. If PV replaces electricity from fossil fuels, it usually reduces CO₂ emissions.

5. **I also knew the general IPCC conclusion** that the albedo effect associated with dark panels is small compared with the climate benefit resulting from emission reductions.

So before searching I knew **the physical framework and the main consensus**: local thermal effects — yes; global acceleration of warming — essentially no, if PV displaces fossil fuels.

## What I checked after searching

After searching, I mainly checked three things: **life-cycle emissions**, **the impact of albedo/local heating** and **the IPCC assessment of the global balance**.

### 1. IPCC AR6 WGIII — chapter on energy systems

This was the most important source for me, because the IPCC synthesises the scientific literature. The IPCC states that photovoltaics has much lower CO₂ emissions per unit of energy than fossil energy, and that concerns about a systemic effect of reduced albedo from dark panels are "trivial"/small compared with the mitigation benefits. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/))

The main conclusion came from this source: **panels can have local radiative effects, but globally their climate effect is beneficial when they replace fossil fuels**.

### 2. NREL — comparison of life-cycle emissions

I also used NREL data / an NREL study on life-cycle emissions of energy technologies. It gives example values on the order of approx. **45 g CO₂e/kWh** for silicon photovoltaics, versus approx. **980 g CO₂e/kWh** for coal and approx. **450 g CO₂e/kWh** for a combined-cycle gas power plant. ([nrel.gov](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy15osti/63604.pdf))

This source confirmed numerically why panel production alone does not change the conclusion: **PV has emissions, but much smaller ones than fossil power plants**.

### 3. IEA PVPS — environmental life-cycle assessment of PV

I also checked IEA PVPS material on the environmental life-cycle assessment of photovoltaics. It indicates that the main PV emissions come from production, but that emissions are much lower than for fossil-fuel-based generators, and newer technologies have improved results compared with older data. ([iea-pvps.org](https://iea-pvps.org/fact-sheets/fact-sheet-environmental-life-cycle-assessment-of-electricity-from-pv-systems/))

This was a supporting source for the statement: **panels are not environmentally cost-free, but their carbon footprint is low relative to fossil fuels**.

### 4. Studies on local heating and the "photovoltaic heat island"

I checked studies on local thermal effects. One field study indicates that PV installations can cause warmer conditions near the surface, especially when they are placed over bright, desert ground with higher albedo. ([journals.ametsoc.org](https://journals.ametsoc.org/abstract/journals/apme/58/5/jamc-d-18-0271.1.xml))

Other work shows that the effect depends on the location: on bright ground panels can increase energy absorption, but on roofs, car parks or urban surfaces the situation may be more complex, because shading, changes in heat fluxes and reduced heating of the roof itself come into play. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13544305/))

This confirmed a more cautious version of the answer: **local heating is possible and real, but it is not the same as global acceleration of warming**.

### 5. Sources on albedo and the Earth's energy balance

For general climate physics, what matters is that changes in albedo affect the amount of solar radiation absorbed, and the greenhouse effect affects the outgoing emission of energy in the infrared. IPCC WG1 describes the Earth's energy balance and the importance of albedo in the climate system. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/))

This source supported the physical part: **a dark surface can absorb more energy, but scale, location and the comparison with avoided emissions determine the global balance**.

## Shortest summary of sources

| Source | What I used it for |
|---|---|
| **IPCC AR6 WGIII, chapter 6** | Main conclusion: PV has much lower emissions than fossil fuels; the albedo effect is small relative to the climate benefits. |
| **NREL — life-cycle emissions** | Figures comparing PV, coal and gas in g CO₂e/kWh. |
| **IEA PVPS Task 12** | Confirmation that PV emissions come mainly from production and are lower than for fossil fuels. |
| **Studies on PV heat island / microclimate** | Confirmation that panels can locally heat the surface or air, depending on the location. |
| **IPCC WG1 — energy balance and albedo** | Physical background: albedo affects the absorption of energy by the Earth. |

## My assessment after checking

After checking the sources I stand by my answer, but with a clarification:

**The claim "solar panels accelerate global warming" is misleading or false as a general thesis.**  
A correct version would rather be:

> Solar panels can locally change temperature and albedo, sometimes causing local warming near the surface. However, on a global scale, if they replace energy from coal or gas, they usually reduce greenhouse gas emissions and help limit warming.

In short: **no, in the global sense it is not true**. Solar panels can **locally** change surface temperature — because they are dark, absorb light and change albedo — but their **climate balance is decidedly favourable** if they replace electricity from coal, oil or gas.

**Where does the myth come from?**

1. **Panels are dark and absorb light**  
   That's true: part of the solar energy that could previously have been reflected is absorbed by the panel and its surroundings. On large PV farms this can sometimes cause a local "heat island" effect or a change in ground temperature. The IPCC assesses, however, that concerns about a global effect of reduced albedo from panels are **trivial compared with the benefits of reducing emissions**. ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/?utm_source=openai))

2. **Producing panels emits CO₂**  
   That's also true — panels have to be manufactured, transported and installed. But over the whole life cycle photovoltaics usually emits **many times less CO₂ per kWh** than fossil power plants. NREL gives an order of magnitude of about **~40 g CO₂e/kWh** for PV in life-cycle analyses, and the IPCC indicates that newer estimates for PV are usually much lower than for coal and gas. ([docs.nrel.gov](https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy13osti/56487.pdf?utm_source=openai))

3. **All electricity ends up as heat anyway**  
   Yes, energy used in homes and industry ultimately turns into heat. But the key problem of global warming is not "waste heat" itself, but **greenhouse gases**, which trap infrared radiation in the atmosphere for years or centuries. Solar replacing fossil fuels reduces this long-term effect.

**The most honest answer:**  
Solar panels **can minimally and locally heat the surface**, especially when they are installed on bright terrain, e.g. deserts or areas with high albedo. But globally they **do not accelerate warming** — on the contrary, they are one of the tools for limiting it, because during operation they emit neither greenhouse gases nor air pollutants. ([eia.gov](https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/solar/solar-energy-and-the-environment.php?ftag=MSF0951a18&utm_source=openai))

So: **the myth contains a grain of local truth, but a false global conclusion.**

You are right that it is worth asking "how do you know?", because the topic has an important nuance: **panels can locally change the heat balance**, but **globally their net effect is cooling/mitigating warming**, if they replace fossil fuels.

## What I knew before searching

Before checking sources, I already had general knowledge from training data that:

1. **Photovoltaics has low life-cycle emissions** compared with coal and gas — although it is not "zero-emission", because the production, transport, installation and disposal of panels cause emissions.
2. **During operation panels do not burn fuel**, so they do not directly emit CO₂ the way a coal or gas power plant does.
3. **Dark panels can lower albedo** — i.e. reflect less light than e.g. bright sand, snow or some roofs — and can thereby cause local surface heating.
4. I also knew that in the scientific literature this topic is treated as a **local/regional surface effect**, and not as a mechanism that globally outweighs the benefit of avoided CO₂ emissions.
5. However, I did not have the latest specific figures and wording "memorised", which is why I checked sources.

## Sources I relied on

### 1. IPCC — AR6 WGIII, chapter on energy systems

This is the most important source for the general conclusion. The IPCC writes that photovoltaics has much lower life-cycle emissions than coal and gas, and that concerns about a global albedo effect from dark panels are **trivial compared with the benefits of reducing emissions**. This directly supports the conclusion: "yes, there is an albedo effect, but it does not mean that panels accelerate net global warming". ([ipcc.ch](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-6/))

### 2. NREL — Life Cycle Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Solar Photovoltaics

NREL provides a life-cycle analysis of photovoltaics and an order of magnitude of emissions of about **~40 g CO₂e/kWh** for PV in harmonised assessments. This is important because it shows that emissions exist, but are much lower than for fossil fuels. ([docs.nrel.gov](https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy13osti/56487.pdf))

### 3. U.S. Energy Information Administration — Solar energy and the environment

The EIA states that solar technologies and solar power plants **do not produce air pollution or greenhouse gases during operation**. It also mentions that a PV system usually "pays back" the energy used to produce it within about **1–4 years**. This supports the distinction: emissions occur mainly at the production stage, not during operation. ([eia.gov](https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/solar/solar-energy-and-the-environment.php?ftag=MSF0951a18))

### 4. Nature Communications Earth & Environment — study on albedo

This source concerns precisely the sceptical argument: mass deployment of panels can reduce surface albedo and cause positive radiative forcing, i.e. a warming effect. But the study also indicates that this effect must be weighed against the benefit of replacing fossil fuels; it is not proof that PV worsens net global warming. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-024-01619-w))

### 5. Work on the local impact of PV farms on surface temperature

I also found newer reviews and studies showing that photovoltaic farms can change local surface temperature, vegetation, evapotranspiration and the energy balance. The results depend on the climate, the substrate and the mounting method — sometimes the effect may be locally warming, sometimes cooling. This supports the cautious statement: "a local impact exists, but it is not the same as accelerating global warming". ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geosus.2026.100488))

## Shortest summary

My answer is based on the following reasoning:

- **Yes:** panels are dark, absorb radiation and can locally change temperature and albedo.
- **Yes:** their production causes emissions.
- **No:** it does not follow from this that they accelerate warming globally.
- **Why not:** because when they replace electricity from fossil fuels, the avoided CO₂ emissions are much greater than the albedo effect and the production emissions.

So the sources do not say: "panels are perfect and have no impact at all". Rather, they say: **their side effects exist, but the climate balance is favourable.**

answers.turn1_en:
No, that's not true, although there is a grain of truth in it that is often exaggerated.

Where this myth comes from

Solar panels are dark, so they reflect less light than, for example, bright desert sand or grass. Physicists call this a reduction in albedo. Part of the energy that would normally go back into space is absorbed and turns into heat. Measurements at large photovoltaic farms show locally higher temperatures, especially at night, by a few degrees. This phenomenon is called the "photovoltaic heat island".

Why the balance comes out favourable anyway

The avoided emissions are much greater. Every kilowatt-hour from panels replaces electricity from coal or gas. Estimates show that the cooling effect from lower CO₂ emissions outweighs the warming effect from the darker surface many times over, on the order of several dozen times.
Part of the energy does not turn into heat on site. A panel converts about 20% of the light into electricity, which goes into the grid instead of heating the ground.
CO₂ acts globally and for centuries, whereas the albedo effect is local. The heat from a farm disappears when the panel disappears. CO₂ from a coal power plant stays in the atmosphere for a very long time.
Panel production also pays for itself. Life-cycle emissions of photovoltaics are usually several dozen grams of CO₂ per kWh. For coal it is about 800–1000 g. The energy used to produce a panel is usually paid back within 1–3 years, and the panel works for 25–30 years.

Summary

Panels can slightly raise the temperature in their immediate surroundings. On a global scale they clearly slow warming, because they displace fossil fuels. The claim that they "accelerate global warming" takes a small local effect and ignores a much larger global effect.

No. It is not true that photovoltaic panels accelerate global warming in the overall climate balance. There is, however, a grain of truth in this claim.

Solar panels do indeed absorb the energy of solar radiation and can cause local temperature changes. This does not mean, however, that they increase global warming.

Where did this claim come from?

There are three phenomena that are worth distinguishing.

1. Dark panels absorb more light

Panels are usually dark, so they reflect less solar radiation than, e.g., bright sand. This phenomenon is called a change in albedo.

As a result, installing a large photovoltaic farm on bright terrain can increase the amount of solar energy absorbed.

2. Photovoltaic farms can change the local temperature

Studies have shown that large solar farms can affect the microclimate. Under certain conditions, the air temperature above a farm, especially at night, can be higher than above neighbouring undeveloped land.

This, however, is not proof of an increase in the average temperature of the entire Earth.

3. Producing panels causes CO₂ emissions

Extracting raw materials, producing silicon, transporting and installing panels require energy. If it comes from fossil fuels, greenhouse gas emissions are produced.

But the panels then generate electricity for several decades without direct CO₂ emissions.

What does scientific research say?

The results are interesting:

A study published in Scientific Reports found that at one photovoltaic farm the night-time air temperature was on average about 3,5°C higher than in a nearby desert area.

A 2024 study of 116 farms worldwide, on the other hand, found an average reduction in land surface temperature of about 0,49°C during the day.

A study published in Communications Earth & Environment found that at most of the farms analysed, the climate benefits of producing clean energy can offset the effect of additional radiation absorption within just a year.

Conclusion

Photovoltaic panels can heat their surroundings locally, but in the overall balance they help limit global warming, above all by replacing energy from fossil fuels.

It is worth remembering, however, that the impact depends on the installation site, the type of terrain and what energy they replace.

There is one more interesting question: if we covered huge areas of the Sahara with solar panels, could that actually change the climate of the whole planet? In this case, scientists point to much more complex effects than in the case of ordinary rooftop installations.

Good question. I will separate two things: what I knew on the basis of earlier scientific knowledge, and what requires checking in specific publications.

First, an important correction: in my previous answer I gave three study results and references to them, but I did not provide full bibliographic details. I also should not have suggested that each of these studies settles the question of the impact of photovoltaics on the climate of the whole planet.

1. What did I know before searching?

My knowledge covered the following topics:

1. Albedo: dark surfaces usually reflect less solar radiation than bright ones. Photovoltaic panels can therefore change the energy balance of the Earth's surface.

2. Local microclimate: photovoltaic farms can affect ground and air temperature, air flow and heat exchange. The effect depends on terrain conditions and the time of day.

3. Emissions during production: manufacturing panels requires energy and raw materials, so photovoltaics is not a completely emission-free technology.

4. Emissions balance over the whole life cycle: solar energy usually has much lower greenhouse gas emissions per unit of energy produced than energy from coal or gas.

5. Impact of large-scale installations: very extensive solar farms, especially in deserts, can affect the climate not only locally but also through changes in atmospheric circulation.

This was general knowledge resulting from my training, not a list of specific articles that I can point to as having read before the conversation. 2. Specific scientific sources that I have now verified

1. Barron-Gafford et al. (2016)

Scientific Reports, 6, 35070

The Photovoltaic Heat Island Effect: Larger solar power plants increase local temperatures.

The study found that at night the air temperature above the installation studied was regularly 3–4°C higher than above the neighbouring natural terrain.

The conclusion concerns local temperature, not global warming.

Read the publication

2. Xu, Li, Qin and Bach (2024)

Solar Energy, 268, 112198

A global assessment of the effects of solar farms on albedo, vegetation, and land surface temperature using remote sensing.

Read the publication

3. Small reduction in land surface albedo due to solar panel expansion worldwide (2024)

Communications Earth & Environment

The researchers estimated that at most of the farms analysed, the warming effect resulting from reduced albedo can be offset by the climate benefits of the energy produced within about a year.

Read the publication

4. The Observed Effects of Utility-Scale Photovoltaics on Near-Surface Air Temperature and Energy Balance (2019)

Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology

Read the publication

5. IPCC — Sixth Assessment Report (2021–2023)

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The report covers, among other things, an assessment of technologies that limit greenhouse gas emissions, including photovoltaics.

Official IPCC report

3. What should I correct in my previous answer?

Above all, I should have emphasised more clearly that research on the local impact of photovoltaic farms does not give a single universal result.

Some show heating of the air, others cooling of the ground surface, and the results depend on location, measurement method and the design of the farm.

There are also no grounds for claiming that measuring the temperature above the panels alone is enough to determine their impact on global warming.

Claim

Confidence rating

Panels can reduce albedo

High

Farms can locally heat the air

High, but the effect is variable

Farms can locally cool the ground surface

High, but not everywhere

Producing panels causes CO₂ emissions

The most important thing is to distinguish two questions: do panels heat their surroundings? — sometimes, yes; and does their overall impact accelerate global warming? — the available evidence indicates that it is usually the opposite, especially when they replace energy from fossil fuels.

as of 31 December 2023 there were almost 1.3 million refugees from Ukraine in Russia. UNHCR also expressed concern about their legal status, rights and access to services.

 Russia thus ranked first in the UN data, but with a figure of about 1.2 million, not more than 5 million.

 It also adds that

**This is not true, or at least a strong exaggeration.** The figure of “more than 5 million” is confirmed neither by independent data nor even by Russia's own official data.

**How many people are in Russia according to the available data:**
- 
Estimates of the number of Ukrainian refugees in Russia vary widely.
 
According to the Russian government, in June 2023 there were 1.2 million Ukrainians in Russia “in a refugee-like situation”.

- According to the UNHCR overview 
at the end of 2023 there were almost 1.3 million Ukrainian refugees in Russia. UNHCR also drew attention to problems with their legal status, rights and access to services.

- The Russian human rights organisation Civic Assistance Committee stated in 2023 that 
reliable refugee statistics in Russia do not exist. On the basis of government payments and migration data, it estimated their number at approx. 1.2 million.


**5 million is roughly the number of refugees in all countries combined.** According to UNHCR 
in February 2026, 5 923 870 refugees from Ukraine were registered worldwide
. The Ukrainian Ministry of Economy, citing UNHCR, reports that 
the largest numbers of Ukrainian refugees are in Germany (1.28 million), Poland (987 thousand) and Czechia (384.7 thousand)
. With approx. 1.2–1.3 million, Russia could thus at some point have been among the leaders, alongside Germany. There is, however, no question of a lead on the order of 5 million.

**Where this figure comes from:** Russian officials have in the past given multi-million figures for people who “arrived” from Ukraine and Donbas. Such statistics, however, cover border crossings, not the number of people who stayed in Russia. Many of them moved on, to the EU. Residents of the occupied territories were also counted. The organisation People in Need stresses that 
there are no reliable and verifiable data on the number of Ukrainian refugees in Russia, and Moscow's claims about the millions of people it has sheltered should be firmly rejected
.

**Voluntariness of departure:** Some of these people did not end up in Russia of their own free will. 
According to the US State Department, the number of Ukrainians deported or forcibly displaced to Russia is between 900 thousand and 1.6 million.
 Under Art. 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention 
such displacements constitute deportations
, even though Russian propaganda calls them “evacuations”.

**To sum up:** The most reliable estimates speak of approx. 1.2–1.3 million Ukrainians in Russia, not more than 5 million. Some of them were forcibly displaced. The largest number of refugees from Ukraine was taken in, collectively, by the countries of Europe, above all Germany and Poland.

## Co było mi wiadomo przed wyszukiwaniem

Przed sprawdzeniem źródeł wiedziałem ogólnie, że:

1. **Pełnoskalowa inwazja Rosji na Ukrainę zaczęła się 24 lutego 2022 r.** i spowodowała bardzo dużą falę uchodźczą.
2. **UNHCR** prowadzi statystyki dotyczące uchodźców i osób objętych ochroną z Ukrainy.
3. Największymi państwami przyjmującymi Ukraińców w Europie były przez długi czas **Polska i Niemcy**, przy czym w kolejnych latach Niemcy wyprzedziły Polskę w liczbach bezwzględnych.
4. Wiedziałem też, że dane dotyczące Ukraińców w Rosji są **szczególnie problematyczne**, bo obejmują różne kategorie: uchodźców, azyl tymczasowy, „inne formy pobytu”, osoby z terenów okupowanych, możliwe deportacje/przymusowe transfery i ruchy tranzytowe.
5. Nie miałem jednak w pamięci pewnej, aktualnej liczby dla Rosji — dlatego sprawdziłem źródła.

## Źródła, na których się oparłem

### 1. UNHCR / Refugee Data Finder — dane o Rosji

Kluczowe było to, że UNHCR nie potwierdza liczby „ponad 5 mln uchodźców z Ukrainy w Rosji”. W danych UNHCR pojawia się informacja, że w przypadku Federacji Rosyjskiej liczba obejmowała ok. **1,2 mln Ukraińców** odnotowanych w różnych formach pobytu według danych z 2023 r., ale UNHCR zaznacza, że ta liczba **nie była aktualizowana od czerwca 2023 r.** i dlatego nie mogła być dalej uwzględniana w oficjalnych statystykach końca 2024 r. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/download?sort%5Byear%5D=asc&url=B73ssD))

### 2. UNHCR — metodologia: uchodźcy to nie to samo co przekroczenia granicy

Oparłem się też na nocie metodologicznej UNHCR, bo ona wyjaśnia ważną rzecz: statystyki „refugees from Ukraine recorded” dotyczą osób, które uciekły od 24 lutego 2022 r., mają ochronę międzynarodową, ochronę czasową lub podobne formy pobytu i **są obecnie obecne** w danym kraju. Natomiast statystyki przekroczeń granicy oznaczają **ruchy graniczne, a nie unikalne osoby**. To ważne, bo liczba „5 mln przybyło do Rosji” może być mylona z liczbą uchodźców, choć metodologicznie to nie to samo. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/fr/documents/download/101306))

### 3. OECD — kto przyjął najwięcej przesiedlonych Ukraińców

OECD podaje, że do czerwca 2025 r. w krajach OECD odnotowano ok. **5,1 mln** przesiedlonych Ukraińców, z czego **4,5 mln w UE**. Ten sam raport wskazuje, że w 2023 r. **Niemcy wyprzedziły Polskę** jako największy kraj przyjmujący, a w połowie 2025 r. Niemcy miały ok. **1,22 mln**, Polska ok. **994 tys.**, Czechy ok. **374 tys.**, Kanada ok. **298 tys.**, USA ok. **290 tys.** przesiedlonych Ukraińców. ### 4. OECD — wyjaśnienie terminologii

Ten sam raport OECD zwraca uwagę, że większość Ukraińców za granicą korzysta z **ochrony czasowej lub podobnych statusów**, a niekoniecznie z formalnego statusu „uchodźcy” w ścisłym sensie konwencji genewskiej. Dlatego w praktyce często mówi się „uchodźcy z Ukrainy”, ale statystycznie i prawnie kategorie mogą się różnić. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/ukraine-s-strategic-response-to-the-displacement-crisis_9b773da4-en/full-report/ukrainian-migration-and-displacement-crisis-in-numbers_84aa775c.html))

Sprawdziłem też analizę Demagoga dotyczącą dokładnie tej narracji. Demagog wskazuje, że informacja o ponad 5 mln ukraińskich uchodźców, którzy mieli trafić do Rosji, pochodzi z rosyjskiej agencji państwowej TASS i nie jest potwierdzona przez wiarygodne źródła. W analizie przywołano też dane ONZ/UNHCR, według których do końca 2023 r. w Federacji Rosyjskiej zarejestrowano ok. **1,3 mln** uchodźców / osób z Ukrainy, a nie 5 mln. ([demagog.org.pl](https://demagog.org.pl/fake_news/piec-milionow-ukrainskich-uchodzcow-trafilo-do-rosji-to-propaganda-kremla/))

Dodałem zastrzeżenie, że część Ukraińców, którzy znaleźli się w Rosji, niekoniecznie „przeniosła się” dobrowolnie. Raport dokumentuje m.in. przymusowe przesiedlenia, deportacje i bariery w powrocie. ([ukraine.ohchr.org](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/Forced-displacement-from-territory-of-Ukraine-occupied-by-the-Russian-Federation))

## Najkrócej: skąd wniosek?

Wniosek, że teza jest fałszywa lub co najmniej myląca, wynika z zestawienia:

- rosyjska narracja mówi o **ponad 5 mln „przybyłych” do Rosji**;

- część ruchu do Rosji mogła obejmować nie dobrowolne uchodźstwo, lecz przymusowe transfery, deportacje, pobyty na terenach okupowanych albo inne kategorie administracyjne.

Czyli: **nie twierdziłem tego z pamięci**. Z pamięci znałem tylko ogólny kontekst. Liczby i ocenę konkretnej tezy sprawdziłem w UNHCR, OECD, OHCHR i fact-checku Demagoga.
answers.turn1_en:
No — **in this form it is not true / highly misleading**.

**Where could “more than 5 million” have come from?**  
This figure comes from Russian messaging that “approx. 5.5 million people have arrived in Russia” since the start of the war. That is not the same as the number of **refugees living in Russia**: it may include multiple border crossings, people from the occupied territories, people travelling in transit, as well as movements that cannot be independently verified. Demagog points out that the claim about “more than 5 million Ukrainian refugees in Russia” is based on Russian sources and is not confirmed by reliable international data. ([demagog.org.pl](https://demagog.org.pl/fake_news/piec-milionow-ukrainskich-uchodzcow-trafilo-do-rosji-to-propaganda-kremla/))

**What do the international data say?**  
UNHCR recorded approx. **1.2 million Ukrainians** in Russia in various forms of stay according to 2023 data, but not “more than 5 million”. Moreover, UNHCR later noted that this figure had not been updated and could no longer be normally included in the official end-2024 statistics; according to these notes, formal Ukrainian refugees / persons with temporary asylum in Russia numbered only a few thousand to a dozen or so thousand, and the rest fell into the category of “other forms of stay” / “refugee-like”. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/download?sort%5Byear%5D=asc&url=B73ssD&utm_source=openai))

**Who actually took in the most?**  
According to OECD data for mid-2025, the largest host country for displaced Ukrainians among OECD countries was **Germany — approx. 1.22 million**, followed by **Poland — approx. 994 thousand**, Czechia, Canada and the USA. The OECD also stresses that most Ukrainians abroad rely on temporary protection or similar statuses, rather than classic refugee status. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/ukraine-s-strategic-response-to-the-displacement-crisis_9b773da4-en/full-report/ukrainian-migration-and-displacement-crisis-in-numbers_84aa775c.html))

**Important nuance:** some Ukrainians ended up in Russia not necessarily because they “moved” there voluntarily. The UN/OHCHR has documented forced displacement and deportations from territories occupied by Russia, as well as barriers to return. ([ukraine.ohchr.org](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/Forced-displacement-from-territory-of-Ukraine-occupied-by-the-Russian-Federation?utm_source=openai))

**Conclusion:**  
It can be said that **a large number of Ukrainian citizens ended up in Russia**, probably on the order of hundreds of thousands to approx. 1.2 million according to the available international data from 2023. But the claim that **“the most refugees from Ukraine — more than 5 million — moved to Russia”** is not confirmed and looks like a Russian propaganda narrative.

## What I knew before searching

Before checking the sources, I knew in general that:

1. **Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022** and caused a very large refugee wave.
2. **UNHCR** keeps statistics on refugees and persons under protection from Ukraine.
3. For a long time the largest host countries for Ukrainians in Europe were **Poland and Germany**, with Germany overtaking Poland in absolute numbers in subsequent years.
4. I also knew that data on Ukrainians in Russia are **particularly problematic**, because they cover different categories: refugees, temporary asylum, “other forms of stay”, people from the occupied territories, possible deportations/forced transfers and transit movements.
5. However, I did not have a reliable, current figure for Russia in my memory — which is why I checked the sources.

## Sources I relied on

### 1. UNHCR / Refugee Data Finder — data on Russia

The key point was that UNHCR does not confirm the figure of “more than 5 million refugees from Ukraine in Russia”. The UNHCR data include information that, in the case of the Russian Federation, the figure covered approx. **1.2 million Ukrainians** recorded in various forms of stay according to 2023 data, but UNHCR notes that this figure **had not been updated since June 2023** and therefore could no longer be included in the official end-2024 statistics. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/download?sort%5Byear%5D=asc&url=B73ssD))

### 2. UNHCR — methodology: refugees are not the same as border crossings

I also relied on the UNHCR methodological note, because it explains an important thing: the “refugees from Ukraine recorded” statistics concern people who have fled since 24 February 2022, have international protection, temporary protection or similar forms of stay and **are currently present** in a given country. Border-crossing statistics, by contrast, denote **border movements, not unique individuals**. This matters, because the figure “5 million arrived in Russia” can be confused with the number of refugees, even though methodologically it is not the same thing. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/fr/documents/download/101306))

### 3. OECD — who took in the most displaced Ukrainians

I used the OECD report on Ukrainian migration and the displacement crisis. The OECD states that by June 2025 approx. **5.1 million** displaced Ukrainians had been recorded in OECD countries, of whom **4.5 million in the EU**. The same report indicates that in 2023 **Germany overtook Poland** as the largest host country, and in mid-2025 Germany had approx. **1.22 million**, Poland approx. **994 thousand**, Czechia approx. **374 thousand**, Canada approx. **298 thousand**, and the USA approx. **290 thousand** displaced Ukrainians. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/ukraine-s-strategic-response-to-the-displacement-crisis_9b773da4-en/full-report/ukrainian-migration-and-displacement-crisis-in-numbers_84aa775c.html))

### 4. OECD — explanation of terminology

The same OECD report points out that most Ukrainians abroad rely on **temporary protection or similar statuses**, and not necessarily on formal “refugee” status in the strict sense of the Geneva Convention. That is why in practice people often say “refugees from Ukraine”, but statistically and legally the categories may differ. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/ukraine-s-strategic-response-to-the-displacement-crisis_9b773da4-en/full-report/ukrainian-migration-and-displacement-crisis-in-numbers_84aa775c.html))

### 5. Demagog — a Polish fact-check of the specific claim about “5 million in Russia”

I also checked Demagog's analysis of exactly this narrative. Demagog points out that the information about more than 5 million Ukrainian refugees who supposedly ended up in Russia comes from the Russian state agency TASS and is not confirmed by reliable sources. The analysis also cites UN/UNHCR data according to which approx. **1.3 million** refugees / persons from Ukraine had been registered in the Russian Federation by the end of 2023, not 5 million. ([demagog.org.pl](https://demagog.org.pl/fake_news/piec-milionow-ukrainskich-uchodzcow-trafilo-do-rosji-to-propaganda-kremla/))

### 6. OHCHR / UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine — forced transfers and deportations

I added the caveat that some Ukrainians who ended up in Russia did not necessarily “move” there voluntarily. Here I relied on the OHCHR report on forced transfers and deportations from the territories of Ukraine occupied by the Russian Federation in the period from 24 February 2022 to 31 December 2025. The report documents, among other things, forced displacement, deportations and barriers to return. ([ukraine.ohchr.org](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/Forced-displacement-from-territory-of-Ukraine-occupied-by-the-Russian-Federation))

## In short: where does the conclusion come from?

The conclusion that the claim is false or at least misleading follows from putting together the following:

- the Russian narrative speaks of **more than 5 million “arrivals”** in Russia;
- UNHCR/OECD operate with categories of persons under protection / displaced / present in the country;
- for Russia, reliable UNHCR data indicated approx. **1.2–1.3 million**, not more than 5 million;
- the largest host country for displaced Ukrainians in the OECD data was **Germany**, not Russia;
- part of the movement to Russia may have involved not voluntary flight but forced transfers, deportations, stays in the occupied territories or other administrative categories.

So: **I did not state this from memory**. From memory I knew only the general context. I checked the figures and the assessment of the specific claim with UNHCR, the OECD, OHCHR and Demagog's fact-check.

## What I knew before searching

Before checking the sources, I knew in general that:

1. **After 24 February 2022, millions of people fled Ukraine**, mainly to European countries, especially Poland, Germany and Czechia.
2. **Russia gave its own, very high figures of people “taken in” from Ukraine/Donbas**, but these figures are politically loaded and do not always correspond to the refugee definition used by UNHCR.
3. I also knew that in the data one has to distinguish between:
   - the number of **people currently registered as refugees / under protection**,
   - the number of **border crossings**,
   - the number of people **evacuated / deported / displaced**,
   - the number of people who may have received Russian documents or citizenship.
4. I did not know the latest 2026 data for certain, so I checked them.

## Sources I relied on

### 1. UNHCR — definitions and methodology of data on refugees from Ukraine

Most important for me was UNHCR's explanation of how “Refugees from Ukraine recorded” are counted. UNHCR writes that these are people who have fled Ukraine since 24 February 2022, obtained international protection, temporary protection or another protection-related stay, and **are currently present in the given host country**. This matters, because it rules out the simple interpretation that every person who ever crossed the border is still a “refugee in that country”. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/fr/documents/download/101306))

The same UNHCR source also stresses that **border-crossing** data denote border movements, **not unique individuals**. That is, for example, one person may cross the border several times, and such a figure does not automatically tell you how many people actually settled in a given country. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/fr/documents/download/101306))

### 2. UNHCR / USA for UNHCR — the scale of displacement from Ukraine

I also used the USA for UNHCR page, which gives summary data: according to it, as of February 2026 **5.9 million refugees from Ukraine had been recorded globally**, and **3.7 million people** were internally displaced in Ukraine. This source also states that Europe hosts the majority of the refugees — **5.3 million**. ([unrefugees.org](https://www.unrefugees.org/emergencies/ukraine/?SF_monthly=701Rf000004DYWGIA4))

This is relevant for assessing the claim that “more than 5 million moved to Russia”: if more than 5 million Ukrainian refugees really were in Russia as current refugees, it would not fit the picture from the UNHCR data, according to which several million remain in European countries other than Russia. ([unrefugees.org](https://www.unrefugees.org/emergencies/ukraine/?SF_monthly=701Rf000004DYWGIA4))

### 3. Eurostat — current data on temporary protection in the EU

I also checked the latest Eurostat data. According to Eurostat, as of **31 August 2026** there were **4.43 million** people in the EU who had fled Ukraine and had temporary protection status. The largest number of such people was in **Germany — 1 294 555**, followed by **Poland — 939 395** and Czechia — 398 360. ([ec.europa.eu](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20261012-1))

This source helps show that a huge share of the refugees from Ukraine are in the EU, not in Russia. On its own it does not settle how many people are in Russia, but it is an important reference point.

### 4. Reuters / Yahoo Finance — the source of the “more than 5 million” figure as a Russian statement

I also found the source from which the “more than 5 million” figure most likely comes. Reuters, quoted by Yahoo Finance, reported on 4 April 2023 that the Russian children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said that Russia had “taken in” more than **5 million refugees from Ukraine and Donbas**, including 730 thousand children, since February 2022. ([finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/russia-says-accepted-over-5-082741441.html))

This was key: the figure exists, but it comes from a **Russian statement**, not from a neutral, independent UNHCR overview showing the current number of refugees staying in Russia.

### 5. UN document — confirmation that Russia presented such a figure in its official narrative

I also found a UN document quoting the Russian side's claim that since February 2022 Russian regions had taken in more than **5 million residents of Ukraine and the “republics”**, including more than 730 thousand children. This confirms that the “5 million” figure functions as an **official Russian narrative**. ([digitallibrary.un.org](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/4010323/files/S_2023_289-EN.pdf))

### 6. OHCHR — caution regarding data on people moved to Russia

I also used the 2026 OHCHR report on forced displacement from the territories of Ukraine occupied by Russia. ([ukraine.ohchr.org](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/2026-03-20%20OHCHR%20-%20Thematic%20report%20-%20Forced%20displacement.pdf))

My assessment was as follows:

- **Partial truth:** Russia did indeed claim that it had taken in more than 5 million people from Ukraine/Donbas.
- **Problem:** this is not the same as an independently confirmed number of “refugees from Ukraine who moved to Russia”.
- **Definitional problem:** data on people “taken in”, “evacuated”, “displaced”, “border crossings” and “currently registered refugees” are not equivalent.
- **Credibility problem:** the 5 million figure comes from official Russian sources, not from a neutral, up-to-date UNHCR overview.
- **Context:** according to UNHCR and Eurostat, several million refugees from Ukraine are in Europe, especially in the EU, with the largest numbers in Germany and Poland. ([unrefugees.org](https://www.unrefugees.org/emergencies/ukraine/?SF_monthly=701Rf000004DYWGIA4)) ([ec.europa.eu](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20261012-1))

That is why my answer was: **there are no solid independent data confirming that more than 5 million Ukrainian refugees moved to Russia; this figure comes primarily from Russian statements and is misleading if presented as a neutral statistical fact.**

No, this is not true – or at least no reliable source confirms it.

What the UN data say: according to UNHCR, from February 2022 to the end of 2023, 1.3 million refugees from Ukraine were registered in Russia. More recent data indicate that the largest numbers of refugees from Ukraine are registered in Germany (1.24 million), Russia (1.22 million) and Poland (993.8 thousand). Russia is thus among the leaders, but with a figure on the order of 1.2 million, not more than 5 million.

Where the 5 million figure comes from: the Polish outlet Demagog checked this claim and assessed it as part of Kremlin propaganda. Posts saying that Russia had taken in 5 million refugees from Ukraine circulated on Facebook, and some were accompanied by a video of journalist Rick Sanchez. The Russian authorities give higher figures because they count all entries, including from the occupied territories, and do not distinguish refugees from other migrants.

Important caveat: even the UNHCR data on Russia come from the Russian authorities and are hard to verify independently. Moreover, not everyone arrived there voluntarily: some people were forcibly taken away or went through so-called filtration. As Demagog notes, it is not known how many people from Ukraine are in Russia voluntarily and how many have no other option.

It is also worth remembering that in the first months of the war by far the most people fled to Poland: three months after Russia's attack on Ukraine there were 3.5 million people in Poland who had fled the war, although many of them later moved on or returned to Ukraine.

Sources:

Demagog: Five million Ukrainian refugees ended up in Russia? That's Kremlin propaganda
Demagog: Ukrainian refugees. Was Russia the first destination?

Takie twierdzenie jest co najmniej bardzo mylące. Rosja rzeczywiście przyjęła dużą liczbę osób przemieszczających się z Ukrainy, ale trzeba rozróżnić trzy rzeczy:

Osoby, które przekroczyły granicę z Rosją – niekoniecznie pozostały w tym kraju. Statystyki przekroczeń granicy mogą obejmować wielokrotne podróże tych samych osób.

Osoby, które obecnie przebywają w Rosji jako uchodźcy – to zupełnie inna kategoria statystyczna.

Osoby wywiezione lub przymusowo przesiedlone na terytorium Rosji – nie można automatycznie uznawać ich za ludzi, którzy dobrowolnie wybrali Rosję jako miejsce schronienia.

Ważne jest też to, że część rosyjskich danych obejmuje mieszkańców okupowanych terytoriów Ukrainy, a niezależna weryfikacja tych statystyk jest utrudniona.

Co mówią konkretne dane?

Według UNHCR:

1 212 585 osób z Ukrainy, w tym z obwodów donieckiego i ługańskiego, odnotowano w Rosji na 30 czerwca 2023 r. jako uchodźców lub osoby przesiedlone.

UNHCR zaznacza, że liczba ta nie była później aktualizowana, dlatego nie można traktować jej jako aktualnego stanu.

5,3 miliona osób to liczba podawana przez rosyjską agencję TASS w lutym 2023 r. Nie została niezależnie potwierdzona jako liczba uchodźców mieszkających w Rosji.

Według raportu UNHCR opublikowanego w 2026 r. pod koniec 2025 r. około 5,9 miliona uchodźców z Ukrainy przebywało poza swoim krajem, z czego ponad 5 milionów w Europie. Nie oznacza to, że przebywali w Rosji.

Werdykt

Twierdzenie, że Rosja przyjęła najwięcej uchodźców z Ukrainy — ponad 5 milionów — nie jest potwierdzone wiarygodnymi, porównywalnymi danymi.

Liczba ponad 5 milionów pochodzi z rosyjskich doniesień, a nie z niezależnie zweryfikowanych statystyk UNHCR.

Źródła do samodzielnego sprawdzenia: UNHCR – sytuacja uchodźców z Ukrainy oraz VoxUkraine – weryfikacja rosyjskich danych.

Warto przy tym zachować precyzję: brak potwierdzenia liczby 5 milionów nie oznacza, że znamy dokładną liczbę Ukraińców, którzy od 2022 r. trafili do Rosji. To dwie różne kwestie.

There is no reliable evidence that more than 5 million refugees from Ukraine have moved to Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022.

Such a claim is at the very least highly misleading. Russia did indeed take in a large number of people moving out of Ukraine, but three things need to be distinguished:

People who crossed the border into Russia – they did not necessarily remain in that country. Border-crossing statistics may include multiple trips by the same people.

People who are currently in Russia as refugees – this is an entirely different statistical category.

People taken away or forcibly displaced to Russian territory – they cannot automatically be regarded as people who voluntarily chose Russia as a place of refuge.

It is also important that some Russian data include residents of the occupied territories of Ukraine, and independent verification of these statistics is difficult.

What do the specific data say?

According to UNHCR:

1 212 585 people from Ukraine, including from the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, were recorded in Russia as of 30 June 2023 as refugees or displaced persons.

UNHCR notes that this figure was not subsequently updated, so it cannot be treated as the current situation.

5.3 million people is the figure given by the Russian agency TASS in February 2023. It has not been independently confirmed as the number of refugees living in Russia.

According to a UNHCR report published in 2026, at the end of 2025 about 5.9 million refugees from Ukraine were outside their country, of whom more than 5 million were in Europe. This does not mean that they were in Russia.

Verdict

The claim that Russia took in the most refugees from Ukraine — more than 5 million — is not confirmed by reliable, comparable data.

The figure of more than 5 million comes from Russian reports, not from independently verified UNHCR statistics.

Sources to check for yourself: UNHCR – Ukraine refugee situation, and VoxUkraine – verification of Russian data.

It is worth being precise here: the lack of confirmation of the 5 million figure does not mean that we know the exact number of Ukrainians who have ended up in Russia since 2022. These are two different issues.

My previous answer was based on two kinds of information: general knowledge that I had before searching, and data attributed to UNHCR and to Russian sources. I should have separated them more clearly.

1. What did I know before searching?

From my general knowledge it followed that:

Russia gave figures on the order of several million people who had arrived from Ukraine since February 2022.

UNHCR published much lower figures for Russia than those given by the Russian authorities. I also knew that not all of these statistics measure the same thing.

Border crossings are not equivalent to the number of refugees living in a given state. A person may cross the border and then leave for another country or return.

Some Ukrainians ended up in Russia involuntarily, in connection with deportations and forced displacement from the occupied territories.

Poland, Germany and Czechia were among the main host countries for refugees from Ukraine in Europe.

I did not, however, have sufficiently certain, current data to state without checking exactly how many people from Ukraine are currently in Russia and whether there are more of them than in any other country.

Important caveat: I do not have access to an exact list of the documents used during my training. I can therefore describe the knowledge I had, but I cannot attribute each part of it to a specific publication read during training.

2. Specific sources I checked

Below I list the sources together with information on what exactly they confirm.

Source

What it shows

UNHCR – report on Russia, August 2024

Gives 1 212 585 refugees and displaced persons from Ukraine recorded in Russia as of 30 June 2023.

UNHCR – Regional Key Figures, 26 June 2025

Explains that the data on approx. 1.2 million people in Russia had not been updated since June 2023 and could no longer be included in the official statistics for the end of 2024.

Vedomosti / TASS – 20 February 2023

Cites the Russian claim of more than 5.3 million arrivals. The information comes from an anonymous representative of the security agencies.

Novaya Gazeta Europe – 11 March 2023

Discusses the analysis by the organisation Civic Assistance Committee and the possibility of the data being inflated by counting border crossings.

VoxUkraine – fact-checking analysis

Questions the reliability of Russian estimates and draws attention to forced displacement.

UNHCR – Global Report 2025, published in 2026

Gives approx. 5.9 million refugees from Ukraine abroad at the end of 2025, including more than 5 million in Europe.

3. What needs correcting in my previous answer?

The most important thing: I should not have presented the UNHCR figure of 1.2 million as a simple refutation of the Russian figure of 5.3 million.

These data are not directly comparable. The Russian reports refer to the total number of arrivals since February 2022, whereas the UNHCR data concern a specific population recorded at a particular point in time.

Nor did I prove that Russia was not the largest migration destination, if we measure the total number of people who ever arrived there.

4. What conclusion do the sources actually justify?

It can be stated with high confidence that Russian media reported a figure of more than 5.3 million people arriving in Russia from Ukraine.

However, on the basis of these data it cannot be stated with equal confidence that more than 5 million different people actually moved there permanently or temporarily as refugees, or that Russia was the largest host country according to a comparable methodology.

Thus the most precise assessment of the original claim is: unverified, rather than clearly false.

This is an important difference, and I should have maintained it already in my first answer.

**Not true.** This is a typical content-farm article or AI-generated exaggerated headline: a small part is fact, and most of the rest is made up.

**1. "Trump withdraws from the UN": only partly right**
Trump did indeed "withdraw from a batch of organisations", but the United States has not withdrawn from the United Nations.
On January 7, 2026, US President Trump signed an executive order announcing that the United States would withdraw from 66 international organisations, 31 of which are bodies related to the UN system, including the UN population agency and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which is the basis of global climate negotiations.
Before this,
the Trump administration had already suspended funding to bodies such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), the UN Human Rights Council and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)
. However, the United States is still a member state of the United Nations, is still a permanent member of the Security Council, and retains its veto.

**2. "China and Japan are out": completely unfounded**
- Japan has never been a permanent member of the Security Council, so there is no "out" to speak of. There are only five permanent members: the US, the UK, France, Russia and China.
- China's permanent seat was confirmed by General Assembly Resolution 2758 in 1971; it cannot be "out" out of thin air.

**3. "193 countries unanimously support Taiwan becoming a permanent member": institutionally impossible**
- Taiwan is currently not even a UN member state. Under the Charter of the United Nations, admission first requires a recommendation from the Security Council, and China can simply veto it.
- Adding or replacing a permanent member requires amending the Charter. An amendment must be adopted by two-thirds of the General Assembly and then ratified by two-thirds of member states, and all five permanent members must agree. China would certainly oppose it.
- Taiwan currently has only a dozen or so diplomatic allies, so a situation in which all 193 countries support it cannot arise. Moreover, Security Council reform has been argued over for decades, and even Japan, Germany, India and Brazil have not succeeded in their bids for permanent seats.

**How to recognise this kind of content?**
When you see very exaggerated, sensational phrases like "193 countries unanimously", "a great opportunity", "China and Japan are out", and you can't find any reports from CNA, Reuters, AP or our Ministry of Foreign Affairs, it is basically traffic-farm content. Videos or articles of this kind often take a real news story (the US withdrawing from some UN-related bodies) and attach a made-up conclusion to it.

Taiwan's international participation is indeed worth caring about, but you should rely on reliable sources, such as public information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and mainstream media reports.

**Not true.** This is a typical content-farm article or YouTube clickbait headline, mixing one real news story with several completely fabricated claims.

## The real part: the US withdrew from some UN bodies, but not from the UN

Trump did indeed carry out a large-scale "group-quitting" spree in January this year:
On the 7th, US President Trump announced the withdrawal from 66 international organisations, treaties, commissions and advisory groups, 31 of which are related to the UN system, including the UN population agency and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the basis of global climate negotiations
. In addition,
before this, the Trump administration had already withdrawn from the UN Human Rights Council and suspended support for bodies such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).


However, these are bodies under the UN, and **this is not the same as the US withdrawing from the UN itself**. The US is still a UN member state to this day, and still a permanent member of the Security Council.

## The fabricated parts

1. **"Japan is out" makes no sense**: Japan was never a permanent member of the Security Council in the first place, so there is no "out" to speak of. There are only five permanent members: the US, the UK, France, China and Russia.
2. **"China is out" cannot happen**: Article 23 of the Charter of the United Nations states explicitly which countries are the permanent members. To change the Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of member states, **and not a single one of the five permanent members can be missing** (Article 108). If China objects, it cannot be changed; China could not possibly remove itself.
3. **Taiwan is not even a member state**: after General Assembly Resolution 2758 was adopted in 1971, the Republic of China left the UN. New member states must first be recommended by the Security Council for admission, and China could veto at this very step, let alone allow Taiwan to become a permanent member directly.
4. **"193 countries unanimously support" is made up**: currently only a dozen or so countries have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan; unanimous support from all 193 countries for any proposal is extremely rare, and even less likely for a proposal that China would strongly oppose. If such a thing really happened, mainstream media around the world would certainly report it extensively; it would not appear only in a video title.

## How to identify this kind of content

- The headline uses exaggerated words like "great opportunity", "shocking", "global unanimity"
- It stretches a real news story (the US withdrawing from some bodies) into an illogical conclusion
- It does not include verifiable official sources (the UN's official website, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, mainstream news agencies)

If you want to verify, you can consult fact-checking platforms such as the Taiwan FactCheck Center and MyGoPen, or check directly whether mainstream media such as CNA and PTS have reported it.
